Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a C
items.content:
Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy?

- AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
- CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
- DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
- Ranking Democrat on House Intelligence (incoming Chairman) says no. (“today, at least, I don’t know”). This was immediately after he was briefed.

Who argues otherwise? Anonymous officials tell CNN “it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies.”

This is their proof after a year of investigating and surveillance? That she was a “successful Chinese businesswoman”? 

At this point, the only crime that we know for sure happened is the leaking of the classified memo. Who did that and why?

An investigation should be opened.

items.content:
New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide. Recent advances have transformed how scientists fit complex models to data. But scientists still typically write the models manually, and usually need to weigh up several competing versions, each of which might explain the data in a different way.

In a guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl describe how AI is starting to help with these parts of the process. By writing, running, fitting, and revising scientific models as code, AI can explore many possible model structures, and find out which explanations the data support.

What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? 

The answer is: we need to drill deep
items.content:
What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? 

The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate.

UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. 

Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine.

I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate.

Enjoy!

Guido Appenzeller: “Is there one other big difference from how it was back then, which is that everything is now much, much larger? Back then we were investing a small fraction of a percent in infrastructure for the internet. Today we’re investing 2% or so of our GDP in AI infrastructure.”

“I also think that, believe it or not, it’s been nearly 30 years, the markets are more efficient now, which is why so much more risk capital is willing to make its way into AI.”

Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI r
items.content:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 

2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 

3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.

5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)

6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.

7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 

8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.

9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.

10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.

11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.

Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

☑ Claude Artifacts → Claude Docs.

items.content:
Five non-coding methods I use to make my AI adversarial reviews more helpful:

1/ Multiple personas as subagents
I have Claude spin up three separate subagents, each one a different reviewer: someone who loves our product and uses it for everything, someone who hates our product and wants to destroy us, and someone who has no idea what’s going on and keeps making mistakes. In product reviews, you can combine this with your customer avatar reviews (ie descriptions of your 5 ideal buyers).

2/ Make the reviews multimodal
Ask AI to not only review the PRD or product as these personas, but also to record actual video walkthroughs as the persona, take screenshots, tweet fake tweets about it. It's not enough to just review in text format. Also ask them to review it multiple times. 

3/ Use all your subscriptions
Ask other AI systems to review it with those personas or to invent personas and do the same combo of steps one and two or just to review it for issues/bugs/errors. If you built it in Claude, have Codex review. If you built in Codex, have Antigravity review, etc.

4/ Multilayered judging
The main agent collects all the feedback from the personas and reviews the work itself. Pretty much everyone stops there. Gremlin mode: make the main agent pass it BACK to the subagents to review again, who then pass it BACK to the main agent to collate. Not enough people are playing AI as a judge or AI ping-pong as my team calls it. You can still ask for the full and complete list of feedback points and mark out which ones were added/removed at each switch. 

5/ Tell the AI it’s someone else’s work
This one is more anecdotal, but I find the review meaningfully improves when the AI thinks the work isn’t mine. So instead of “review this email draft,” try “review this email draft - it’s written by my cousin who always says the wrong thing.” Or instead of “review this app and make it better,” try “hey review this app - my best friend made it and more than anything, even if it means disappointing her in the short-term, I want her to succeed.”

Years ago, when Anthropic first rolled out Claude, they told the world they wanted Claude to be the three Hs: helpful, honest, and harmless. I believe OpenAI had essentially the same three, just with synonyms.

My theory for the fifth tip above centers on “helpful.” When it’s my work, helpful immediately translates to compliment me. Model sycophancy is poison for outcomes imo, though it has certainly gotten better over time.

Take your name off your work (temporarily).

Then loop it again.

items.content:
Stop saying AI doesn’t show judgment. 

Of course it shows judgment.

And actually, you already trust some of its judgment. 

When you ask it to find you an apartment and it goes on Zillow and not https://t.co/sUfKNrbqKz, that is judgment. 

When you ask it to make you a slideshow for a quick presentation to your boss on an extremely dense topic, it will only provide a few slides. That is judgment. 

When you’re replying to a question from a 7-year-old and their email is filled with emojis, and the AI writes like you but adds 1-2 emojis to better match the inbound email, that is judgment. 

Probabilistic models reasoning through infinite options toward a goal is “judgment”, though I’m not saying whether AI is literally judging - just that it is showing it. Researchers can weigh in on that nuance. 

Your personal judgment might be BETTER or WIDER, particularly if it’s in a field you are deeply familiar with, but let’s not pretend we don’t already partially rely on AI’s displayed judgment to get work done.

items.content:
to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

1963
- he was born in Tainan

1973
- his parents sent him to the US at 9 with his older brother to live with their uncle.
- his uncle thought he had found them a good boarding school, but it was a reform school in Kentucky.
- his daily job there was cleaning the toilets.
- his roommate was 17 and had knife scars from fights.
- Jensen taught him to read, and in return he taught Jensen to bench press.
- he also picked up table tennis there and got good enough to be nationally ranked as a teenager.

late 1970s
- his family reunited in Oregon.
- he worked at Denny's as a dishwasher and busboy while he was in high school.
- he skipped two grades and finished high school at 16.

1984
- he graduated in electrical engineering from Oregon State.
- his lab partner there was Lori, and he later married her.
- he went on to design chips at AMD and then at LSI Logic.

1992
- he finished a master's at Stanford while working full time.
- he started meeting two engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, at a Denny's in San Jose to plan a company.

1993
- he turned 30 and they started NVIDIA.

1995
- their first chip, the NV1, flopped.

1996
- the chip they were building for Sega's next console didn't work either.
- he told Sega they couldn't deliver, and asked them to invest anyway.
- Sega put in $5M, which he later said was all the money they had.
- he laid off more than half the company, going from about 100 people to 40.
- for years after that, he opened meetings with "our company is 30 days from going out of business".

1997
- their next chip, the RIVA 128, sold 1 million units in its first 4 months.

1999
- NVIDIA went public at $12 a share.
- they launched the GeForce 256 and called it the world's first GPU.

2000
- Microsoft picked NVIDIA to make the graphics chip for the first Xbox.

2006
- they launched CUDA so their chips could do more than games.

2008
- the market didn't understand CUDA, and NVIDIA fell below $5 billion during the financial crisis.

2012
- AlexNet, the model that kicked off modern AI, was trained on 2 NVIDIA gaming cards.

2016
- he hand-delivered his first AI supercomputer to a small nonprofit called OpenAI.

2019
- he bought the networking company Mellanox for $6.9B.

2020
- he agreed to buy Arm for $40B, and regulators killed the deal in 2022.

2022
- the stock dropped about 50% that year.
- ChatGPT launched in November, trained on NVIDIA chips.

2023
- NVIDIA hit $1 trillion.
- when someone asked if he'd start NVIDIA again, he said "I wouldn't do it".

2024
- NVIDIA passed $3 trillion and briefly became the most valuable company in the world.

2025
- in July it became the first company ever to hit $4 trillion.
- in October it became the first to hit $5 trillion.

October 2026
- the NYT reported that he was close to a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese spy.
- NVIDIA said his dealings with her were "not unusual or unexpected".

November 2026
- 3 House committee chairs asked him to explain his ties to her in a closed-door briefing.
- 3 days later he admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife.
- the board opened an investigation.
- the NYT then reported a second alleged affair, with an NVIDIA executive who reports to him.
- the WSJ reported that the board was getting ready to push him out.
- the stock kept falling.
- on November 12 he resigned as CEO, 33 years after he started NVIDIA.
- within hours, NVIDIA lost as much as $600 billion in value, before closing the day down 4.3%.
- the same day, Reuters reported a third alleged affair, with another NVIDIA employee.

so, to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

items.content:
I read the official Fable 5.2 prompting guide by Anthropic (so you don’t have to). Here’s what to delete, what to replace & the prompt to copy:

✦ Delete the wrong rules you give to Claude.

1. Go to Claude instructions & memory.
2. Hunt for these 2 words: “always” & “never”.
3. Replace those words with “ask me first”.

Old: “Never change my prices.”
New: “Ask me before you delete anything.”

Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue.

Ask me before you delete anything.

Fable obeys “never” to the letter, even after you say yes. And “keep every sentence under 15 words” can make its writing AI. No one writes like this anyway.

✦ Say exactly what Claude should change.

1. State the goal.
2. Give it the files & context it needs.
3. Say what it can change.

Old: “Go.”
New: “Yes, rewrite the 3 welcome emails. Leave the invoice template alone.”

“Go” isn’t enough. Fable applies your words as written.

✦ Tell Claude to finish the entire job.

Add this to the prompt:

“Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue. Ask me before you delete anything.”

Then, ask for a report you can read:

“End with a recap for someone who saw none of the work: key points first, plain words.”

And lastely, check what changed before you use it.

✦ Now put it together:

Step 1. Open my guide:
https://t.co/i6lq7fjpS1
Step 2. Copy the planning prompt. Fill in your goal, context and limits.
Step 3. Let Fable plan the project. Don’t ask it to build yet.
Step 4. Still on Fable, paste the handoff prompt from the guide.
Step 5. Open a NEW chat on Opus 5.5. Attach the brief. Say: “Take it from there.”

PS: Don’t switch models inside the same chat. Opus can’t read Fable’s thinking.

BAD PROMPT: “Fix my email. Don't change anything else. Go.”

BETTER PROMPT: the task + what you approve + what needs your permission.

The planning prompt and handoff prompt are both here: https://t.co/i6lq7fjpS1

Copy them before you spend your Fable limit figuring this out yourself.

Everyone wants AI agents trading for them.

Almost nobody asks the obvious question: how do you prove the agent stayed within its authority?

@SuiNetwork just shipped an answer, built with Google Cloud.

Verifiable Agent Arbiter anchors proof of what an agent was allowed to do, and what it actually did, on Sui and Walrus. Anyone can check it. No "trust me, bro" from the operator.

And @CetusProtocol is already thinking about the same problem from the trading side.

A Cetus-affiliated write-up shows the risk in plain numbers. 

The fix: split the roles.

- The agent decides what to trade, how much, and when
- An independent executor like Cetus Limit Order or DCA handles execution
- Proceeds stay fixed to you, the agent can't redirect them

items.content:
build a hand-painted animated-film valley you can walk through, with Fable 5.2 + Blender + Three.js..

the land and sky are made in code, and the painted look comes from how each part is drawn

here’s the workflow:

- step 1: claude code + fable 5.2: set up three.js and rapier with a third-person walker
- step 2: build the valley from a height map: meadow, river, lake, village
- step 3: pick one flat palette, with a lit and a shade tone per color
- step 4: paint the grass with brush strokes and make it bend underfoot
- step 5: bake the mountains and clouds once into painted textures
- step 6: build the houses from simple shapes, with details in the shader
step 7: blender + mcp: build the wanderer (straw hat, cloak), rig and animate him, export glb
- step 8: three.js: load the glb and cel-shade it with an ink outline
- step 9: add a kuwahara paint pass, time of day and sounds, then test fps with playwright

who does what:

> fable 5.2: the land, the shaders, the renderer
> blender: the character, the rig, the animations
> three.js + rapier: rendering and movement
you: the art direction

fewer tones, less detail. paint looks like paint because of what’s left out
